title: 2024 Smart-Meter Electricity Consumption Report
executive_summary: Analysis of 1,428 cleaned smart-meter readings for 2024 shows total consumption of 1,207,700 kWh across 12 meters. Industrial buildings dominate usage, accounting for over 82% of all consumption. Consumption dipped mid-year before recovering strongly in Q4, and the second half of the year was 4.7% higher than the first. Peak and off-peak tariffs are nearly evenly split. Commercial buildings show a moderate negative correlation between temperature and energy use on hot days.

key_findings.statement: The dataset contains 1,428 readings with a combined consumption of 1,207,700 kWh and a mean of 845.7 kWh per reading.
Industrial buildings consumed the most energy at 995,362 kWh (82.4% of total), followed by Commercial at 196,367 kWh (16.3%) and Residential at 15,971 kWh (1.3%).
Quarterly consumption peaked in Q4 (352,882 kWh), followed by Q1 (319,678 kWh), Q2 (270,277 kWh), and Q3 (264,863 kWh), indicating a mid-year trough and a strong year-end recovery.
Second-half consumption (617,745 kWh) exceeded first-half consumption (589,955 kWh) by 4.7%, representing an increase of approximately 27,790 kWh.
On hot days (temperature ≥ 25 °C), 19 commercial readings were recorded with a mean consumption of 415.3 kWh per reading.

The median consumption across all readings is 406.8 kWh with a sample standard deviation of 913.4 kWh, indicating high variability. The mean recorded temperature is 11.6 °C, with 62 readings missing temperature data. For commercial buildings, the Pearson correlation between temperature and consumption is -0.64, suggesting that higher temperatures are associated with lower commercial energy use.

Off-peak tariff consumption (608,076 kWh) slightly exceeds peak tariff consumption (599,624 kWh); peak usage accounts for 49.7% of total consumption. Across 12 distinct meters, the highest-consuming single meter recorded 252,241 kWh.

limitations: 62 readings are missing temperature data, which may introduce bias into temperature-based analyses, particularly the commercial correlation and hot-day filtering.
The residential segment contains only 15,971 kWh across very few readings, making building-type comparisons unbalanced and residential insights less reliable.
With only 12 distinct meters, meter-level findings (e.g., highest-use meter) may not generalise to a broader portfolio.
Hot-day commercial analysis is based on just 19 readings, limiting statistical confidence in the mean consumption estimate.
The analysis covers a single calendar year (2024); year-on-year trend comparisons are not possible without prior-year data.
conclusion: Industrial consumption dominates the portfolio and should be the primary focus for efficiency initiatives. The Q4 surge and H2 uplift of 4.7% warrant investigation into seasonal or operational drivers. The near-equal peak/off-peak split suggests limited tariff optimisation opportunity, though the highest single-meter usage of 252,241 kWh merits targeted review. Addressing missing temperature records would strengthen future thermal-load modelling.
